The city’s smallest public building stood between a locksmith and a bakery. Its sign read:

**DEPARTMENT OF UNFINISHED THINGS**

It opened at nine, closed at four, and observed all municipal holidays.

People arrived carrying the usual objects: half-knitted scarves, application forms, novels with bookmarks stranded near the beginning. A man once brought a staircase. He had built seven steps in his garden before admitting that he didn’t know what he wanted to reach.

The clerk accepted everything.

Her name was Ada. She wore wool cardigans and had a method for untangling necklace chains that nobody had ever successfully copied.

“Will you be wanting this back?” she asked each visitor.

Some said yes immediately. Others asked how much storage cost.

“Nothing,” Ada said. “But we may contact you.”

In the back room, unfinished things occupied tall shelves. Some required special containers. An unsaid apology could stain ordinary cardboard. A plan to move to the coast needed ventilation; otherwise, the whole room smelled of seawater. Promises made to children were kept away from the radiator.

Every Thursday, Ada wrote letters.

*Dear Mr. Bell,*

*Your guitar has been here for eleven years. Yesterday it made a noise when I opened the window. I thought you should know.*

Or:

*Dear Ms. Ortiz,*

*The blue sweater now requires only one sleeve. You left the needles in it, and the yarn has kept well. We are open Saturday this month.*

She did not write *Time is running out*. She had found that people rarely responded usefully to that.

One winter morning, a boy came in with empty hands.

“I think I left something,” he said.

“What sort of thing?”

“I don’t remember.”

Ada gave him a claim form.

The boy studied the boxes.

“I can’t fill this out.”

“Then we’ll look.”

They passed the shelf of abandoned languages, which murmured quietly in its sleep. They passed several ambitions to become doctors, a large collection of exercise plans, and a box marked **DANCES LEARNED FOR WEDDINGS THAT DID NOT HAPPEN**.

Near the rear window, the boy stopped.

There was a small wooden boat on the sill.

“That’s mine.”

Ada checked its tag.

“No,” she said. “This belongs to a woman named Eleanor. She began making it when she was seventy-three.”

The boy looked embarrassed.

“But,” Ada continued, “there’s more wood in the cupboard.”

They spent the afternoon cutting a hull. Ada showed him how to hold the knife so that, if it slipped, it would travel away from his hand. He carved slowly. Once he took too much off one side, and they altered the other side to match.

At four, the boat was still unfinished.

“Can I leave it here?” he asked.

“Of course.”

“Will you send me a letter?”

“If you don’t come back.”

He returned the next morning before Ada had taken off her coat.

Years later, when she retired, the city offered to rename the building in her honor. She declined and requested better lighting over the worktable instead.

The request went through three committees.

In the meantime, someone from the bakery brought over a lamp.
